name: BOSNIA

flag.title: Bosnia & Herzeg.
flag.note: Blue field, yellow triangle, white stars

lead: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a mountain country in the Balkans. Mosque towers and church steeples share one skyline. Ottoman bridges stand beside Austro-Hungarian town halls. Emerald rivers run through the valleys. Bears and wolves live in the forests. The capital, Sarajevo, once sparked World War One.

sections.wows: 7 things to make you go wow

geo: The rugged Dinaric Alps cover most of Bosnia. Emerald rivers like the Neretva and the Una cut through them. Snow melts into rapids, perfect for rafting.
The south is Herzegovina. It is drier, with grapes and figs. Bosnia has only 20 km of Adriatic coast. The port of Neum sits in that gap.
animals: Bears, wolves, and lynx all live wild in Bosnia's forests. About 1,000 brown bears roam the mountains. The Eurasian lynx is Europe's largest wild cat.
Vjetrenica Cave shelters blind shrimps and beetles that live nowhere else. Few caves on Earth hold so many kinds of life.
culture: Coffee here is a ceremony. It boils in a copper džezva pot and pours into a tiny fildžan cup. You sip it through a sugar cube.
Ćevapi, small grilled meat rolls in flatbread, are the favourite street food. In old Sarajevo, a mosque, two churches, and a synagogue stand minutes apart.
history: Bosnia was Ottoman from 1463 for over 400 years, then Austrian from 1878. On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. That one bullet set off World War One.
A war tore the country apart in 1992–1995. Sarajevo endured a 1,425-day siege. Afterwards, people rebuilt the Stari Most bridge stone by stone.
wows: Stari Most bridge stood 427 years, fell in 1993, and reopened in 2004.
Bosnia has just 20 km of coast, one of Europe's shortest.
Perućica in Sutjeska National Park is one of Europe's last ancient forests.
Sarajevans dug a secret tunnel under the airport to bring in food.
Bosnia ranks in the world's top 10 for coffee drinking.

myths.myth: Bosnia is still a war zone
myths.fact: The war ended in 1995. Today Sarajevo and Mostar welcome visitors.
The pyramid-shaped hills near Visoko are natural. Experts found no sign that people built them.
